Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- English football star Steven Gerrard has admitted punching a man in a bar, but the Liverpool captain insisted in his court testimony that it was in self-defense. England international Steven Gerrard is in court defending his actions after a bar brawl late last year. The 29-year-old is facing a charge of affray after an incident in the early hours of December 29, when he attacked businessman Marcus McGee following a dispute about the music that was being played. If found guilty, Gerrard faces a maximum penalty of six months in jail and a fine of $7,200. Gerrard, who denies the charge, told a judge on Thursday that he was sorry about his actions in Southport's Lounge Inn, but at the time he thought McGee was going to attack him. They had been involved in an argument after Gerrard tried to change the music on the bar's sound system, but McGee would not let him, the UK Press Association reported. "I thought he was going to hit me," Gerrard said. "He was on his way forward to me and his behavior had changed from when I was having a discussion with him. I didn't know why." Gerrard said he was unaware that his friend John Doran had already punched McGee when he himself started to hit the 34-year-old. "I am certainly mistaken in thinking he was coming towards me to throw punches at me," the midfielder said. "Now I know, obviously, he had been struck, reacted and thought the strike was by me and he came into me and that's when I reacted. I am sorry about the whole incident. "I grabbed the back of his jumper as he moved forward to me. When I had hold of Marcus, I remember swinging my right hand two or three times. "I was trying to stop still and I felt I had arms all over me. I could see a melee around Marcus McGee. When I was getting pulled away I realized people were patting me, some of whom were my friends. "I wanted to help control the situation. I was worried the fight I had with Marcus was going to get worse because people were going past me in that direction." Gerrard said that his friends had earlier told him to "forget" the argument, but he felt he needed to confront McGee. "I couldn't understand why the guy had such a problem with me, why he was so aggressive," he said. "I was also concerned that if I did leave it I would not have been able to enjoy my night, he may have come over to me. "I wanted to see why he had such a problem with it, why a total stranger had such a problem with me putting my favorite songs on. I asked why I couldn't have an input in the music and tried to explain that I had permission from the manageress." "I asked Marcus what was the problem with the music machine and why he treated me like that. Very quickly he came off the bar stool and was in my face right by me." Gerrard had been celebrating after scoring two goals as Liverpool thrashed Newcastle 5-1 to remain top of the Premier League, and admitted that he had been drinking alcohol. "I certainly knew I had had a drink. I was certainly in control of how I felt in my surroundings," he said. The father of two said he had not been in trouble with the police since the age of 19, when he was banned from driving for nine months for drink-driving.

In Gerrard’s later understanding, McGee had reacted after being punched, mistakenly believed Gerrard had delivered the blow and then advanced toward him, prompting Gerrard’s response.

Apologizing for everything that happened, Gerrard said he took hold of the back of McGee’s jumper as McGee came forward and then swung his right hand two or three times. He recalled trying to remain in place while feeling people’s arms around him and seeing a scuffle involving McGee. As he was pulled away, he became aware that several people—including some of his friends—were patting him.

Gerrard said he then wanted to help calm the situation because he feared his confrontation with McGee could escalate as others moved in that direction.

Although his friends had previously urged him to let the disagreement go, Gerrard said he felt compelled to speak to McGee. He could not understand why a stranger seemed so hostile toward him simply for wanting to play his preferred songs. He was also concerned that leaving the issue unresolved would spoil the rest of his evening or that McGee might approach him later.

Gerrard said he asked why he was not allowed to have a say in the music and explained that the venue’s manageress had given him permission. When he questioned McGee about both the music system and the way he had been treated, McGee quickly rose from his bar stool and moved very close to him.

Earlier that day, Gerrard had scored twice as Liverpool defeated Newcastle 5–1, a result that kept the club at the top of the Premier League. He was celebrating the victory and admitted consuming alcohol, but told the court that although he knew he had been drinking, he remained aware of his surroundings and in control of himself.

The father of two also said he had not had any trouble with police since he was 19, when a drink-driving offense resulted in a nine-month driving ban.

# Gerrard Tells Court He Acted in Self-Defence During Lounge Inn Confrontation

**LIVERPOOL —** Liverpool captain Steven Gerrard told a court that he struck a man during a late-night disturbance at Southport’s Lounge Inn because he believed he was about to be attacked.

Giving evidence at Liverpool Crown Court, Gerrard described the confrontation that occurred in the early hours of December 29, 2008, after he had joined friends for a night out following Liverpool’s 5-1 Premier League victory over Newcastle United.

The England midfielder admitted punching businessman Marcus McGee three times but denied a charge of affray. Gerrard said he acted instinctively and in self-defence after McGee approached him during an argument over control of the bar’s music system.

## Dispute over music led to confrontation

The court heard that Gerrard had been celebrating with friends at the Lounge Inn in Southport, Merseyside. During the evening, he asked about changing the music and sought access to a card or control device being used to select songs.

McGee, who had been handling the music, refused the request. Prosecutors said the disagreement escalated and that Gerrard later returned to confront him.

Gerrard told jurors that he initially believed the exchange had ended. However, he said the atmosphere changed when McGee moved toward him and began shouting.

The footballer said he experienced “a wave of panic” because he thought McGee was about to strike him. Gerrard testified that he responded by throwing punches before the wider disturbance unfolded around them.

He maintained that he had not planned to fight and had not been looking for trouble.

## CCTV footage central to the case

Closed-circuit television footage from inside the Lounge Inn formed a central part of the evidence. The recording showed Gerrard and McGee facing each other near the bar before the incident erupted, although parts of the physical exchange were obscured by other people.

The prosecution argued that Gerrard had become involved in a group attack after McGee refused to hand over control of the music. It alleged that the Liverpool captain’s actions went beyond reasonable self-defence.

Gerrard’s legal team disputed that account, saying the footage supported his evidence that the encounter developed suddenly. The defence argued that he had reacted to what he honestly believed was an imminent assault.

Gerrard acknowledged that he had consumed alcohol during the evening but rejected the suggestion that he had been out of control. He told the court that he remained aware of what was happening and had responded only when he felt threatened.

## Footballer questioned over use of force

Under questioning, Gerrard accepted that he had landed three punches. He said the blows came in quick succession and were delivered in the heat of the moment.

The prosecution challenged him on whether that level of force had been necessary, particularly given his physical fitness and experience as a professional athlete. Gerrard insisted that he had not had time to assess the situation calmly.

His testimony focused on his state of mind at the instant McGee approached. In a self-defence case, jurors must consider whether the defendant genuinely believed force was necessary and whether the response was reasonable in the circumstances as he perceived them.

McGee suffered facial injuries during the disturbance, including the loss of a tooth. Gerrard expressed regret that the incident had happened but continued to deny that he had unlawfully participated in violent disorder.

## Night out followed major Liverpool victory

The incident came after Gerrard had scored twice in Liverpool’s emphatic win at Newcastle, a result that strengthened the club’s position in the Premier League title race.

After returning to Merseyside, Gerrard went out with friends and later arrived at the Lounge Inn. What began as a celebration became the subject of a criminal prosecution and intense national attention because of Gerrard’s status as Liverpool and England’s leading midfielder.

Several other men connected with the disturbance entered guilty pleas to affray. Gerrard, however, chose to contest the allegation and give evidence before the jury.

Throughout his testimony, he rejected the prosecution’s portrayal of him as the aggressor. He said he had approached McGee to discuss the earlier disagreement but had not intended to start a fight.

## Jury clears Liverpool captain

After hearing the evidence, the jury found Gerrard **not guilty of affray**. The verdict ended the criminal case against him arising from the Lounge Inn disturbance.

The acquittal meant jurors accepted, or could not rule out, Gerrard’s account that he had acted in self-defence. He left Liverpool Crown Court without a conviction, bringing to a close a case that had placed one of English football’s most prominent players under sustained scrutiny.
